notes.title: Investigating the Reasoning Abilities of Large Language Models for Understanding Spoken Language in Interpersonal Interactions
notes.bp: An interview coach must judge whether a spoken answer addresses the interpersonal question, not merely whether its words are grammatical.
notes.wh: Interview answers depend on context, social intent, turn history, and domain knowledge that surface lexical matching misses.
notes.naive: Ask a general language model to answer from the transcript alone and treat fluent text as understanding.
notes.ap: Evaluate large language models on spoken-interaction reasoning with explicit contextual knowledge and prompt structure.
notes.mech: Supply interview context and domain knowledge, compare prompting strategies and model scales, and score both answer quality and reasoning behavior.
notes.math: Prompt conditions act as information controls: context and domain knowledge reduce ambiguity, while ablations reveal which information supports the decision.
notes.eval: VetTrain interview data are used with quantitative and qualitative evaluation, model-size comparisons, and prompt ablations involving domain knowledge and interaction context.
notes.ww: The paper reports that contextual and domain-knowledge prompting improves selected spoken-interaction reasoning settings, especially for larger models.
notes.po: The paper's payoff is a more explicit account of conversational-grounding; the reported benefit remains author-reported.
notes.limits: Interview distribution, transcript quality, subjective scoring, prompt sensitivity, and model-family coverage limit claims about general conversational understanding.
notes.evidence_boundary: D3 structured analyst note backed by captured PDF/text; result remains author-reported and was not independently reproduced.

notes.title: When Humans Growl and Birds Speak: High-Fidelity Voice Conversion from Human to Animal and Designed Sounds
notes.bp: A voice converter should carry identity and expressive qualities across human, animal, or designed sound domains without collapsing the target sound.
notes.wh: Source and target domains differ in pitch structure, timbre, articulation, and available parallel data.
notes.naive: Copy a human speaker embedding into the target domain or train paired conversion on a narrow set of source and target voices.
notes.ap: Learn high-fidelity cross-domain conversion that preserves controllable identity cues while generating a plausible target-domain signal.
notes.mech: Separate content-like and identity-like evidence, condition generation on the desired target sound, and evaluate both acoustic fidelity and perceptual identity.
notes.math: The conversion mapping must preserve information useful for the target domain while discarding source-domain artifacts; perceptual judgments test whether this tradeoff is believable.
notes.eval: The paper evaluates human-to-animal and designed-sound conversion with objective audio comparisons and listener judgments against conversion baselines.
notes.ww: The authors report improved fidelity and plausibility for cross-domain conversion, while the unusual targets expose failures hidden by ordinary human voice-conversion benchmarks.
notes.po: The paper's payoff is a more explicit account of cross-domain-voice-conversion; the reported benefit remains author-reported.
notes.limits: Sparse target data, subjective evaluation, target-domain definitions, and unclear physical correspondence limit claims of general voice conversion.
notes.evidence_boundary: D3 structured analyst note backed by captured PDF/text; result remains author-reported and was not independently reproduced.

notes.title: Investigating Gender Bias in Text-to-Audio Generation Models
notes.bp: A text-to-audio generator should not turn neutral prompts into systematically gendered sound or reproduce stereotypes as if they were acoustic facts.
notes.wh: Training captions and web audio encode social stereotypes, and a plausible sample can conceal unequal behavior across prompt groups.
notes.naive: Report aggregate generation quality and assume that a named model is neutral unless an obvious failure is heard.
notes.ap: Define a measurable gender-bias audit for text-to-audio outputs and compare model behavior across controlled prompts.
notes.mech: Generate matched prompt sets, classify or rate gendered attributes, and aggregate the results into a bias score that makes asymmetry visible.
notes.math: The audit compares conditional output distributions rather than a single sample; the metric converts a social-risk question into a reproducible disparity measurement.
notes.eval: Multiple text-to-audio systems and controlled prompt sets are evaluated with the proposed gender-bias metric and qualitative inspection.
notes.ww: The paper reports frequent gender bias that reflects training-data stereotypes and argues for explicit bias evaluation in text-to-audio systems.
notes.po: The paper's payoff is a more explicit account of generative-bias-audit; the reported benefit remains author-reported.
notes.limits: Gender labels, annotator assumptions, prompt coverage, model versions, and the proposed metric's validity limit causal or cultural conclusions.
notes.evidence_boundary: D3 structured analyst note backed by captured PDF/text; result remains author-reported and was not independently reproduced.

notes.title: Discrete Audio Representations for Automated Audio Captioning
notes.bp: An audio captioner must preserve sound events in a compact representation while giving a language decoder enough evidence to describe them.
notes.wh: Audio contains simultaneous events and fine timing, but a caption model must compress it before generating variable-length language.
notes.naive: Use one continuous embedding or a generic tokenizer and assume reconstruction preserves whatever captioning needs.
notes.ap: Compare discrete audio representations for caption generation and test whether tokenization retains semantic evidence.
notes.mech: Encode audio into learned discrete tokens, condition a text decoder on those tokens, and compare tokenizers and decoder choices on caption metrics.
notes.math: Quantization creates a finite vocabulary of acoustic units; the central question is whether the units preserve event identity rather than merely waveform detail.
notes.eval: Experiments on Clotho compare discrete tokenization methods and captioning systems with standard automatic caption metrics and representation ablations.
notes.ww: The paper reports that selected audio tokenizers improve automated captioning quality, showing that representation design affects semantic generation.
notes.po: The paper's payoff is a more explicit account of audio-token-semantics; the reported benefit remains author-reported.
notes.limits: Reference-caption incompleteness, metric proxy limits, dataset scope, and no broad human grounding study limit conclusions about listener usefulness.
notes.evidence_boundary: D3 structured analyst note backed by captured PDF/text; result remains author-reported and was not independently reproduced.

notes.title: Towards Diverse and Efficient Audio Captioning via Diffusion Models
notes.bp: An audio captioner should describe the same sound accurately in several natural ways instead of producing one brittle sentence or repeating training phrasing.
notes.wh: Sound events are ambiguous and captions are one-to-many: several descriptions can be correct while lexical metrics prefer one wording.
notes.naive: Use a deterministic autoregressive decoder and optimize likelihood toward a single reference style.
notes.ap: Use diffusion-based caption generation to model multiple plausible descriptions while retaining event fidelity.
notes.mech: Condition iterative denoising on audio representations, sample candidate text representations, and decode captions whose diversity can be measured alongside quality.
notes.math: Diffusion represents a distribution over possible captions; sampling exposes the tradeoff between semantic accuracy, diversity, and computation.
notes.eval: DAC is evaluated on audio-captioning benchmarks with caption-quality and diversity metrics, efficiency comparisons, and ablations of the diffusion design.
notes.ww: The paper reports stronger caption quality and diversity than comparison systems, with the stochastic decoder offering broader descriptions.
notes.po: The paper's payoff is a more explicit account of diverse-caption-generation; the reported benefit remains author-reported.
notes.limits: Automatic diversity can reward irrelevant variation, sampling cost matters, references are incomplete, and benchmark audio limits transfer.
notes.evidence_boundary: D3 structured analyst note backed by captured PDF/text; result remains author-reported and was not independently reproduced.

notes.title: Position also matters! Separating Same Instruments in String Quartet using Timbral and Positional Cues
notes.bp: A listener should be able to separate same-instrument parts in a quartet when timbre alone is insufficient and room position carries the distinction.
notes.wh: Same instruments have similar spectra, while reverberation and changing seating alter the spatial cues needed to assign each source.
notes.naive: Train a separator on isolated modern music or rely only on instrument timbre, ignoring position and room response.
notes.ap: Use timbral and positional cues and evaluate generalization to a seating arrangement not used for training.
notes.mech: Represent spectral identity together with spatial or positional evidence, then estimate each instrument while preserving the quartet mixture's structure.
notes.math: Separation is an inverse mixture problem: the model uses complementary cues to resolve sources whose timbral likelihoods overlap.
notes.eval: A new reverberant string-quartet dataset tests the proposed separator across seating arrangements against state-of-the-art separation methods.
notes.ww: The authors report competitive or improved separation and transfer to a new arrangement, indicating that positional cues complement timbre.
notes.po: The paper's payoff is a more explicit account of positional-source-separation; the reported benefit remains author-reported.
notes.limits: One quartet domain, limited seating and recording conditions, dataset scale, and source-isolation metrics limit claims about music separation broadly.
notes.evidence_boundary: D3 structured analyst note backed by captured PDF/text; result remains author-reported and was not independently reproduced.

notes.title: Audiobox TTA-RAG: Improving Zero-Shot and Few-Shot Text-To-Audio with Retrieval-Augmented Generation
notes.bp: A text-to-audio system should retrieve acoustically relevant examples when a prompt describes a rare event, without requiring retraining for every new sound.
notes.wh: Zero-shot prompts may be underspecified and generative models inherit gaps and stereotypes from training data.
notes.naive: Generate directly from text with a fixed model and assume its parametric memory covers rare or compositional events.
notes.ap: Add retrieval-augmented conditioning so generated audio can use examples selected from an external datastore.
notes.mech: Retrieve top-k semantically related audio or captions, inject them into the conditioning context, and compare retrieval strategies without changing the generator's core weights.
notes.math: Retrieval changes the evidence available at generation time; matched comparisons test whether external examples improve conditional likelihood and perceptual relevance.
notes.eval: Audiobox TTA-RAG evaluates retrieval variants and zero-/few-shot text-to-audio generation on multiple metrics and curated evaluation sets.
notes.ww: The paper reports improved generation metrics while preserving few-shot and zero-shot operation, with retrieval choice affecting the result.
notes.po: The paper's payoff is a more explicit account of retrieval-grounded-generation; the reported benefit remains author-reported.
notes.limits: Datastore curation, retrieval leakage, metric validity, prompt coverage, and compute/memory cost limit claims about open-world generation.
notes.evidence_boundary: D3 structured analyst note backed by captured PDF/text; result remains author-reported and was not independently reproduced.

notes.title: Efficient and Microphone-Fault-Tolerant 3D Sound Source Localization
notes.bp: A 3D sound-localization system should continue locating sources when microphones are few, fail, or provide unreliable measurements.
notes.wh: Localization depends on spatial geometry and synchronized channels, so a bad microphone can create confident but incorrect direction evidence.
notes.naive: Use every microphone equally and add hardware redundancy whenever a channel fails.
notes.ap: Learn efficient 3D localization with explicit microphone-fault tolerance and fewer input channels.
notes.mech: Fuse spatial cues with a fault-aware weighting or inference rule, detect unreliable channels, and estimate direction without assuming all sensors are healthy.
notes.math: The system treats sensor selection as part of localization: reducing the active array saves computation while robustness prevents one channel from dominating the spatial estimate.
notes.eval: Simulated and measured microphone faults are evaluated for 3D localization accuracy, computational efficiency, and performance as the number of input microphones changes.
notes.ww: The paper reports competitive localization with fewer microphones and improved tolerance to unreliable or unknown faults.
notes.po: The paper's payoff is a more explicit account of fault-tolerant-localization; the reported benefit remains author-reported.
notes.limits: Array geometry, fault simulation, room conditions, source count, and calibration assumptions limit deployment claims.
notes.evidence_boundary: D3 structured analyst note backed by captured PDF/text; result remains author-reported and was not independently reproduced.
